title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë
openingText: 1801—I have just come back from visiting my landlord—the only neighbour I shall have to put up with. This is certainly beautiful country! Nowhere in England, I believe, could I have chosen a place so entirely cut off from the bustle of society. A perfect heaven for a man who hates company—and Mr. Heathcliff and I make an excellent pair to share its desolation. A splendid fellow! He had no idea how warmly I felt towards him when, as I rode up, I saw his black eyes retreat so suspiciously beneath their brows, and when, on hearing my name, his fingers burrowed still deeper into his waistcoat, determined to guard their privacy.
about:
In 1801, a tenant named Lockwood visits his landlord on the Yorkshire moors and mistakes a hostile household for a promising refuge from society. A snowbound night, a name scratched on a window ledge and the housekeeper Nelly Dean’s memories draw him into the history of two neighbouring homes: Wuthering Heights and Thrushcross Grange.

At the centre are Heathcliff, a child brought into the Earnshaw family without a known history, and Catherine Earnshaw, whose attachment to him collides with her wish for social standing. Their story reaches beyond a single courtship. Marriage, education, property and the treatment of children carry its consequences into another generation.

Emily Brontë’s only novel, published in 1847 under the name Ellis Bell, puts these lives inside accounts told by people who have reasons to defend themselves. Lockwood misunderstands what he sees; Nelly remembers events in which she also took part. Keep an eye on who is speaking, and keep the two Catherines distinct: the repeated names are part of the family history.

acclaim.quote: ‘Wuthering Heights’ was hewn in a wild workshop, with simple tools, out of homely materials.
acclaim.source: Charlotte Brontë, “Editor’s Preface to the New Edition of ‘Wuthering Heights’” (1850), final paragraph; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/771/771-h/771-h.htm
acclaim.context: Emily’s sister and the editor of the 1850 edition describes the novel’s rough, forceful artistry. Her preface both defends and criticises the book; this is her assessment, not a claim of unanimous contemporary praise.

whyItMatters.title: The story makes its witnesses answerable
whyItMatters.body: Lockwood records a history that Nelly tells him, but neither stands outside it. His confident mistakes and her accounts of messages carried, withheld or overheard make the telling part of the action. Readers have to weigh a witness’s explanation against what that witness actually does. That demand feels familiar when a disputed event reaches us through competing accounts.

whyItMatters.title: Intimacy is bound to property and rank
whyItMatters.body: Catherine’s choices take shape among distinctions between a servant and a gentleman, a dependent child and an heir, a house someone loves and a house someone owns. The novel follows affection into the practical arrangements that give one person power over another. It remains pointed where housing and family money shape intimate choices today.

whyItMatters.title: The younger generation carries the consequences
whyItMatters.body: Names, households and patterns of treatment recur as the narrative moves from adults to the children in their care. Education, humiliation and small acts of kindness matter alongside the spectacular passions: the later lives have their own possibilities, even under the pressure of inherited quarrels. The question of what families pass on remains immediate today.

angleCards.title: Follow the witnesses
angleCards.text: Notice when Lockwood sees something himself, when Nelly reports it, and when she quotes somebody else. A confident explanation may sit beside evidence that unsettles it.
angleCards.angleObjective: Track the speaker and source of each account; distinguish observation, hearsay and self-justification without treating either main narrator as wholly reliable or wholly false.

angleCards.title: Watch the doors and windows
angleCards.text: Visitors wait outside, children are shut away, and people watch rooms they cannot enter. The two houses give power a physical shape.
angleCards.angleObjective: Follow thresholds, keys and acts of admission or exclusion, connecting them to who controls each household.

angleCards.title: Keep the names distinct
angleCards.text: Catherine, Cathy and Linton can point to different people as the story moves through time. A name repeated across generations can suggest likeness without making two lives identical.
angleCards.angleObjective: Track the two Catherines and the difference between Edgar Linton and Linton Heathcliff, using the current narrator and period to resolve family titles.

angleCards.title: Notice how children learn
angleCards.text: Lessons, books, work, mockery and imitation all shape the children’s prospects. Watch who is allowed to learn and who is encouraged to remain dependent.
angleCards.angleObjective: Trace education and repeated behaviour across generations, keeping coercion, loyalty and kindness distinct.

cast.name: Mr. Lockwood
cast.description: The outsider renting Thrushcross Grange. His confidence in reading other people exceeds his knowledge of this household.

cast.name: Ellen “Nelly” Dean
cast.description: A servant who has known the families since childhood. Her account includes decisions she made as well as events she witnessed.

cast.name: Heathcliff
cast.role: The outsider in the Earnshaw household
cast.description: Brought home as a child by Mr. Earnshaw, he forms an intense bond with Catherine. “Heathcliff” serves as his entire name.

cast.name: Catherine Earnshaw
cast.description: Hindley’s spirited younger sister and Heathcliff’s childhood companion. Her hopes for herself pull in different directions.

cast.name: Edgar Linton
cast.role: The young gentleman at the Grange
cast.description: Isabella’s brother, brought up in comfort at Thrushcross Grange. His manners and position contrast with Heathcliff’s.

cast.name: Isabella Linton
cast.description: A young woman raised at the Grange whose judgments about Heathcliff meet resistance from the people closest to her.

cast.name: Hindley Earnshaw
cast.description: He resents the place Heathcliff occupies in their father’s affections. He is also Hareton’s father.

cast.name: Frances Earnshaw
cast.description: Hindley brings her home after an absence. Nelly knows little about her background and does not readily understand her fears.

cast.name: Hareton Earnshaw
cast.description: Hindley and Frances’s son, encountered by Lockwood at the Heights. His position in the house is easy for the visitor to misread.

cast.name: Catherine “Cathy” Linton
cast.description: Edgar and the elder Catherine’s daughter, whom Lockwood meets as Mrs. Heathcliff. She is a separate person from the Catherine whose childhood Nelly describes.

cast.name: Joseph
cast.role: The old servant at the Heights
cast.description: A long-serving farm worker whose Yorkshire speech, religious judgments and complaints make a distinctive presence in the household.

cast.name: Zillah
cast.description: The servant who helps Lockwood after his encounter with the dogs and finds him a room for the night.
